utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom, precisely, did you learn the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose from those who knew him. Your Honours, may I say something? In my country, in Bosnia, there is no man without a nickname. I also had a nickname. There is no man who is not addressed or referred to by his nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also give a nickname in there, Sikira; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know if that is correct or not. I know they called him Sikirica. Whether he is Sikira or Sikirica, I know that lots of people spoke about him as Sikira, referred to him as Sikira.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also say in that statement that the person of whom you were talking was, in height, between one metre 68 and one metre 70. Do you accept that that is different from what you have told Their Honours today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what I said today, but I stand by my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stand now by the statement? What you told Their Honours earlier on is that he was between one metre 70 and one metre 75. So which do you now say is the correct height for this man, the one you put in your statement or the one which you gave in evidence earlier today, Witness A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: What my statement says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, some of us have a difficulty with the metres. Would you be able to put it into --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have done some rough calculations, and I stand to be corrected if I am not right. One metre 68 to one metre 70 is between 5 foot 5 and 5 foot 6 or thereabouts. I haven't done the calculation for 1 metre 70 to one metre 75 because, as you can imagine, I wasn't expecting that. But I'm going to also put some other information which I can put a figure to, which I'll go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness A, in fact the man you picked out in court today is between 1 metre 83 and one metre 84 tall. Your Honour, the figures for that are 5 foot 11 or thereabouts. What I suggest to you, Witness A, is that the person you have described both today in evidence and in your statement is someone who is different from the man whom you purported to pick out in court today.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the person sitting in this courtroom whom I identified, I vouch with my life that that is the camp commander Sikirica. And as for the metres, you know, for us Bosnians, five, ten centimetres, it's all the same. I really don't have an eye to judge that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like just to move on to another facet of the description which you gave in evidence today. The man you were describing, you told Their Honours had darkish blond hair. Did the man that you saw in 1992 show any signs of having dyed hair in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not notice that. And that is his business, whether he dyed or didn't dye his hair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness A, would you look again at the man you picked out this morning, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, and that is Mr. Sikirica who is now writing something with his pen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... look at him. The question is this: Would you accept that the colour of that man's hair cannot properly be described as darkish blond?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the courtroom in which I am sitting now, Sikirica, the commander of the Keraterm camp is sitting too. Now, Your Honours, I identified that person, and that is the person who is now writing something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to something which happened on the 5th of February of last year, Witness A. Were you interviewed on that date by a man called Nicholas, and I'm sorry if I pronounce his name wrong, Sebire, do you remember that interview, somebody from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it February? In February this year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last year, I think.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that -- well, perhaps I can refresh your memory. Were you shown some photographs on some occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see some photographs. Now I remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that refresh your memory as to what I'm talking about, February of last year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now it comes back to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall looking at a series of people on the photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall telling the person who showed you the photographs that he was -- that Sikirica was not amongst those whom you were looking at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that too, yes. I did not recognise anyone except one who could look like Fustar, but I did not recognise a single individual from the Keraterm camp on those photographs. The only indication that I gave was the camp commander Fustar, and I said there was some indications that one of the individuals could be he.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like now to turn, if I may, please, to the role that the man who you purport to have identified played. Were there occasions when you saw, Witness A, conversations between that person and shift commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you never saw the man, Sikirica, talking to any of the shift commanders that you have named in evidence before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I saw Sikirica standing together with these commanders because it is about 30 metres from my dormitory. I couldn't hear what they were talking about or discussing but, naturally, since he was in the camp with those commanders, he was out to meet with them. That is logical. But what they were talking about, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You cannot say what the content of any single conversation that you observed taking place was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All that you can say is that you observed him talking with the three shift commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not all of them at the same time, but separately, because there were never three commanders on a shift. There could only be two of them when taking over shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All that you can say is that at any one time there was the man you called Sikirica, there was a shift commander, all that you can say is that they were having a conversation, that's the extent of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now, please, Witness A, about something which you said during the course of this morning's evidence. You were being asked by my learned friend, Mr. Ryneveld, about this. You said, and I quote from the transcript, "I could conclude something like this: For instance, when the volunteers were needed, when this truck would come and they, when they were asking for volunteers first, it would start from Sikirica, 15 volunteers, then commander would pass it down to us." Did you mean by that that Sikirica passed on the request for volunteers to the commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to make it absolutely plain, by that answer you mean that Sikirica was different from the commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If Your Honour will just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now, please, Witness A, if I may, to the issue of interrogations. Would this be correct that you did not see any list of prisoners who were to be interrogated being compiled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's implicit in your answer who it was, or do you know who it was who had compiled those lists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- in my opinion, Mr. Sikirica took the list every day whenever the interrogation would start. He would come out of his building, pass by my dormitory, go upstairs to the upper floor carrying with him his black notebook or telephone book. Some ten minutes or so later, the interrogation would start which means that it is quite possible that he had the list with the names of those who were to be interrogated on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The question was this, Witness A: You did not see and you do not know who it was who had created, compiled, the lists of people to be interrogated. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, you did not see the man you have called Sikirica preparing or writing in a notebook or folders or lists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, no, I did not see that. All I saw was a black notebook and an agenda. When he would pass by my dormitory, he would go to the upper floor, and ten minutes later the interrogations would start.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you saw the man you've called Sikirica carrying a notebook or folder, you cannot say what was actually inside any notebook or folder, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, all of what you say about the lists is your assumption, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn next, please, to the killing of the man whose nickname was Car or Car. Can you fix it as to a date how soon that took place after your arrival at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some four or five days later, because I was still in Room 2 and we had not been interrogated. Your Honours, that is how I remember, because, after all, eight years is a long time, that that is when it was, because we were still in Room 2 and we spent there for some ten, 11, 12 days, and after that I was interrogated and moved to Room 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So sometime around the 3rd or maybe the 4th of June would be the correct date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this correct, that this particular person had been or was alleged to have been in possession of a machine-gun at the time of his arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what Zigic said. They said, "Now you carry a machine-gun and see how it is to carry it around and run with it." According to other soldier, he was caught in some stream with a machine-gun. But that is not true. Where would he get a machine-gun from?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether it was true or not, that was the allegation that was made against him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the focus of the reason for his ill-treatment was that allegation, that he had been in possession of a machine-gun; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the reason why he was singled out for ill-treatment which led to his death. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two people involved whom you've named in that, Duca and Zigic, those people were soldiers, were they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uniforms which you associated with the regular military forces? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had many-coloured camouflage uniforms, both of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zigic in particular, but the other man, were not part of the persons who were guarding either the internal part of the -- of Keraterm or the perimeter fence, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to your own personal interrogation, Witness

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you help us about this? Approximately when did it take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was some 11 or 12 days later, I mean after I was brought to the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So sometime around the 11th or 12th of June, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, could be a day more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the persons who interrogated you, two people, one whose name you did not know and one who had been a policeman of some sort before the war, a man called Modic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. He was a traffic warden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were the only people present in the room conducting the interrogation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were two of them, and a soldier stood in front of the door outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we go very briefly into closed session, please? There are some questions I want to ask him which may affect his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness A, I'd like now to ask you what the consequences of your interrogation were, that you were [redacted] in the room where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as briefly as you can, can you give us a description of what your tasks were as you held that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task was if a soldier, for instance, let's say if it was Kole's shift, it would be -- this man should go to be interrogated, so I was there to assist in that. On one occasion I was forced by a soldier to collect some money, and we were unable to collect much. However, he was satisfied. He left us alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn, if I may, briefly, to the incident involving Zejro Causevic. Can you fix a date when that took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall what date it was. I don't know if you will believe me. We did not know when Monday was, Tuesday or Friday, or what time of the day it was. Whatever I'm saying here in terms of time is an approximation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, we understand that. It was many years ago and I'm not criticising you in any way. I just need you to help me, if you can. Would you accept that the date was sometime around the end of June or early July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was rather in early July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as the issue of whether or not medical treatment was available for that man, obviously, according to your evidence, no doctor came. But is it within your knowledge whether a doctor was in fact summoned but did not come despite the summons? Can you say that that didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present when the doctor was summoned. I asked for -- I asked Sikirica and Fustar for help, and whether they called a physician or not, I wouldn't be able to say. I only know that the doctor did not show up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now briefly to the incident involving Mr. Karabegovic. Can you help us with a date as to when that took place, and perhaps you can fix it in relation to when you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remembered that very well. I think that this was between -- in the period between the 20th and the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us about this: He received a food parcel at some stage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a day, it was a night. It was sometime around 11.30 in the evening, and that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wasn't uncommon, was it, for detainees to receive food from outside Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Keraterm, I can tell you that occasionally, prisoners, including myself, did occasionally get some food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And that would happen either by food parcel coming in in the way that this man had a food parcel coming in or by people coming to the perimeter gate and handing stuff through the fence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My late father every morning came to the gate on the bicycle. Every morning he would come. It was -- the distance was about 800 metres to 1 kilometre. One day I waved him off, but he was determined. He was even courageous enough to ask soldiers for cigarettes. In two months I perhaps received three or four of those parcels, and it was during Kole's shift. Whenever I would see my father during Kole's shift, I would get food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me just make it plain, I'm looking at your answer, Witness

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your father would come to the gate and it would be at the gate that you would receive these parcels?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not allowed to go to the gate. Perhaps some of the soldiers would bring it over to us but, for the most part, if they received this food, they would throw it away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did similar things happen to other detainees, that people would come to the gate or to the fence and hand through, to whoever it was, food parcels?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning now to the reasons why Mr. Karabegovic was beaten. Is this correct that those who were beating him were trying to extort money from him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, in his case, that was the reason for his ill treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like to point out, Your Honours, what Mr. Karabegovic did. He worked for the utility company, and he would -- he would go around and collect payments for the water usage by various consumers around the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn now, please, to the beating and death of Besim Hergic. Do you know or have you been told what the reason for his being beaten was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never found that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then, please, to the incident at Room 3. Can you fix a date for when that incident took place as best you can?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was 27 July -- 26, 27 or 28 July. I cannot pinpoint the date because, believe me, we did not know the exact dates or days of the week because it was not long thereafter that we were transferred to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help me about this: The doors of the various rooms, were they -- of all the rooms, that is, were they left open during the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: The door of my room was open throughout the day. In fact sometimes it was -- sometimes it was cold at night so we would close the aluminum door. And since they were barred, we would keep them ajar so that we could get fresh air. The doors to the Room 3 were large aluminum doors without bars. Only Rooms 1 and 2 had bars on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the other rooms? Apart from your own, were they left open during the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the day the door remained open with the exception of Room 3 where people from Brdo were brought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as the incident itself concerning Room 3, although some shots may have entered other rooms, is this right that, in principal, the shooting was directed at that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was shooting which was conducted by either soldiers or members of the TO who had come in from outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I think that the so-called TO carried out this massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this correct, Witness A: That at any time during that incident, those responsible for it could have, if they had chosen, turned the guns on all the other prisoners in all the other rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, such a possibility did exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear from anybody what was alleged or said to have been the reason for the shooting at Room 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about it from any soldier or from anyone, for that matter why these men were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following day, the two people from the shift who had certainly, in one case, tried to prevent what had been taking place, they went to a particular individual who arrived called Zivko Knezevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the way in which those two people conducted themselves, did it appear to you that they were, as it were, reporting to him concerning the incident the night before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two persons certainly did not -- did not report. Instead, they threw away their weapons in the feet of the commander and sat on their motorcycles and sped away from the camp of Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the nature of the incident, would this be a reasonable conclusion to draw that they were throwing their weapons at the feet of this man because he was in some way responsible for what had happened at the camp the night before?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: At some point my friend's suggestions are too leading to be within the realm of speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: But he's inviting speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, I'm inviting him to draw a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, you called the evidence, and in calling the evidence, counsel must be entitled to cross-examine on it. The trouble about calling this sort of hearsay evidence is that it lets in cross-examination about hearsay, and it must be that what is allowed for the Prosecution must be allowed for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I have no issue with the cross-examination on the issue, but my friend has asked for speculation in terms of what was in the mind of the individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's asking about the questions that were asked and the answers that were given. He's entitled to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I just want to -- in a previous answer, the witness has said that these two individuals angrily threw the weapons at the commander's feet. That word "angrily" was not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will take note of that. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to make it clear to the witness, I'm asking you what conclusion would you draw from the scene which you saw of two men angrily throwing their weapons at the feet of this man Knezevic? Did you conclude that that anger was directed at Knezevic because Knezevic appeared to be responsible for the incident? Is that what it looked like to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This wasn't the only occasion when the man Knezevic was to be seen at the camp, Keraterm, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was that morning that I personally saw him for the first time, and I had known him from the civilian life. He was the head of the -- the chief of SUP in the town of Prijedor. And when the trouble start -- he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had been -- he had been retired and then when the trouble started, he reacted -- he resumed his job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from -- I appreciate that you say that this was the first occasion when you personally had seen him. Did you hear from any others, detained at Keraterm, that the man Knezevic was a visitor, even a regular visitor, to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this topic, did you, when you arrived at the camp back at the end of May -- I won't ask that question, sorry. I thought better of that. As a result of the incident, your understanding is that the two guards who had thrown their weapons at the feet of Knezevic were subsequently sent away to go and fight at the front. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything of the role that Zivko Knezevic played in connection with Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After I was released from the camp, I heard that he was in charge of the camp, in Keraterm. And I will tell you what is the basis for this. When I was supposed to leave my town, it was very hard to pass through the Serb roadblocks. There was no international community presence there. We had to make do the best we can -- could. I signed up for a convoy and I called up a friend who was an ethnic Serb, I would not like to mention his name, and he told me that he wishes me good journey. Ten years -- ten minutes later, the phone rang, it was the same friend of mine who said that I had to give up my intention to go because we had been promised that the International Red Cross would help us get out but that was not correct, so I gave up. He said, "Do you know who is escorting the convoy?" I said I did not know. And he said, "Zivko's police who guarded you in the camp." And this is why I believe that he was in charge of the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn now, please, to the closure of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm confident of getting through if you'll allow me to go past 4.00. I'm confident that I can finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we can go to 4.15 with the cooperation of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness A, the closure of the camp -- in fact, is it not right that the date was actually the 5th of August, not the 2nd of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my position that it was the 2nd of August, and it could have been 5th of August, and I'll tell you why. When I was leaving, I did not know what day it -- of the week it was or what date it was. And when I was released from the Trnopolje camp in -- a certificate signed by an ethnic Serb which is kept with the [redacted] police now, his name was Milenko, and it stated that I would not be fighting, that I would not be joining any army, I had to give him 100 marks for this. That certificate said that I was released on the 4th of August. By this certificate I concluded that we had been released from Keraterm on the 2nd of August, because I only spent two days at Trnopolje. Either the certificate is not correct but, believe me, Your Honours, I did not know what day or what date it was when I was released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness A, I'd like to ask you this, please: The buses which you saw the people board and which you believe went to Omarska, at what time of day was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two buses that collected 134 men, this took place at 7.00, 7.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at what time of day was it that you saw those same buses for the next time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the afternoon, around 4.00. As soon as the two buses left the compound, a column of buses entered which then transferred us on to Trnopolje. When I arrived at Trnopolje I saw my friend Sefik, and I told Sefik, "Somebody said [redacted] and it was my sister's son, and I could not even recognise him." Around 4.00 the buses came from Omarska, the same two buses, and Sefik was on one of them, and he said that he had seen blood. I did not see it but Sefik said this. When the last load came, I approached a driver who I knew well, a Serb called Rade, who played soccer, and he -- I asked him what about it. He said they didn't know where they were going. He said, "Most probably to Manjaca," and indeed my brother did end up at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Help Their Honours, please, about this. How long would it take to drive from Keraterm to Omarska, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Keraterm to Omarska, the distance is 25 kilometres. That is 25 to 27 kilometres. Kozarac is 12, then Kamicani. Then you turn to Omarska. And near the inn called Abropov [phoen] and you go to the mine and then two or three kilometres beyond that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just give us an estimate. Would this be fair? Half an hour to three-quarters of a hour to drive from Keraterm to Omarska in a bus? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the bus drove one kilometre per hour, you know how much it would take. I don't know whether it -- the speed was 40 or 60 kilometres per hour, but you can reach Omarska within 20 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long would it take to go from Omarska to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Omarska to Trnopolje, just subtract 12 kilometres because Keraterm to Trnopolje is exactly 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And help us about this: Apart from obviously travelling from Omarska to Trnopolje that day, because you saw the buses there again, you cannot say where the buses went in the morning after leaving Keraterm, can you, of your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can only say that I saw with my own eyes, and that I followed as both buses turned off in the direction of Banja Luka on to the road Banja Luka-Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If Your Honour will just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, can you help me about this, Witness A: It's right, isn't it, that you told the Office of the Prosecutor in November 1995 that you returned to your house after leaving Trnopolje, and you stayed there until March 1993 when you left Prijedor? Would you accept that that is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in my own house. I was released from the camp in August. I was there until March, and I had to leave the Prijedor town because I was pressured. I was even told that my daughter would be raped, so I had to leave my home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But until that pressure was placed upon you, you were able to remain at home without other disturbance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. If Your Honour will just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take the adjournment now. Witness A, you are reminded not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: at 4.05 p.m. to be reconvened on Wednesday the 21st day of March, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 25
